subject: Civil Engineering
title: Rainwater Harvesting
description: A short lesson to help you apply Rainwater Harvesting.

hook.text: Ancient Nabataeans in Petra carved cisterns to capture every drop of desert rain.

buildup.text: Rooftop collection funnels rain into storage tanks. First-flush diverters discard dirty water.

discovery.text: A 1,000 square-foot roof in a 30-inch rainfall area collects 18,000 gallons per year.

twist.text: In some US states, collecting rainwater was once illegal — water rights are complicated.

climax.text: Bermuda requires every home to have a rainwater catchment roof — it's their only water source.

punchline.text: The simplest water supply falls from the sky — just catch it.

quiz.question: Why does Bermuda require rainwater catchment on every home?
options: It reduces stormwater flooding in the islands
Rainwater is the island's only reliable source of fresh water supply
It lowers water utility costs for residents by half

details.summary: Rainwater harvesting captures precipitation from rooftops and other surfaces for storage and use, reducing demand on municipal supply systems and stormwater infrastructure.
details.whyItMatters: Rainwater harvesting reduces potable water demand by 30-50% for non-potable uses while simultaneously reducing stormwater runoff volume. It provides decentralized water resilience during droughts and supply disruptions.
takeaways: A 100 square meter roof captures approximately 80,000 liters annually in areas with 1,000 mm rainfall
First-flush diverters discard the initial dirty runoff from roofs before collection begins
Storage tank sizing balances capture efficiency against capital cost and available space

faq.question: How much water can a typical rooftop rainwater harvesting system provide?
faq.answer: Capture volume equals roof area multiplied by annual rainfall multiplied by a runoff coefficient of about 0.8 for hard roofs. A 200 square meter roof in an area receiving 800 mm annual rainfall captures approximately 128,000 liters per year.

faq.question: Is harvested rainwater safe for non-potable indoor use?
faq.answer: With proper filtration and disinfection, harvested rainwater is safe for toilet flushing, laundry, and cooling. First-flush diversion removes initial contaminated runoff. Sediment filters remove particles. UV disinfection eliminates pathogens. Tank design prevents stagnation.
